mathcounts-potw-2026-07-27-01.title: Multiples of the LCM
mathcounts-potw-2026-07-27-01.body:
5, 7 and 9 are pairwise relatively prime, so the number must be a multiple of $5 \cdot 7 \cdot 9 = 315$. Multiples: 315, 630, 945, 1260. The greatest three-digit one is 945.

**Answer: 945**

mathcounts-potw-2026-07-27-01.title: Work down from 999
mathcounts-potw-2026-07-27-01.body:
A multiple of 5 and 9 ends in 0 or 5 and has digit sum divisible by 9: the largest three-digit ones are 990, 945, … $990 = 7 \cdot 141 + 3$ ✗; $945 = 7 \cdot 135$ ✓.

**Answer: 945**

mathcounts-potw-2026-07-27-02.title: Big digits in the tens place
mathcounts-potw-2026-07-27-02.body:
Put 8 and 6 in the tens places. The options are $84 \times 62 = 5208$ and $82 \times 64 = 5248$. The greatest product is 5248.

**Answer: 5248**

mathcounts-potw-2026-07-27-02.title: Keep the numbers close
mathcounts-potw-2026-07-27-02.body:
With a fixed sum ($80 + 60 + 4 + 2$ is always 146), a product is largest when the two factors are as close as possible. 82 and 64 (difference 18) are closer than 84 and 62 (difference 22), so $82 \times 64 = 5248$ wins.

**Answer: 5248**

mathcounts-potw-2026-07-27-03.title: Abundant numbers
mathcounts-potw-2026-07-27-03.body:
Numbers whose proper divisors add to more than the number are called abundant. A number below 12 would need many divisors; only 6, 8 and 10 have 3 or more proper divisors, and their sums are 6, 7 and 8 — not enough. 12 is the smallest abundant number.

**Answer: 12**

mathcounts-potw-2026-07-27-04.title: Find the digits
mathcounts-potw-2026-07-27-04.body:
No digit can be 0 (product 0, sum positive). Testing small digit sets: $1,1,2,4$ gives sum $8$ and product $8$ ✓; others fail (e.g. $1,1,1,x$: $3 + x \ne x$; $1,1,3,3$: 8 vs 9; $1,2,2,2$: 7 vs 8; $1,1,2,5$: 9 vs 10). Arrangements of 1, 1, 2, 4: $\frac{4!}{2!} = 12$.

**Answer: 12**

mathcounts-potw-2026-07-27-04.title: Bound the digits
mathcounts-potw-2026-07-27-04.body:
No digit is 0. With digits $a \le b \le c \le d$, sum $\le 4d$, so the product $abc \cdot d \le 4d$ means $abc \le 4$. The options for $(a,b,c)$ are $(1,1,1), (1,1,2), (1,1,3), (1,1,4), (1,2,2)$. Solving $a + b + c + d = abcd$: $(1,1,1)$: $3 + d = d$ ✗; $(1,1,2)$: $4 + d = 2d \Rightarrow d = 4$ ✓; $(1,1,3)$: $5 + d = 3d \Rightarrow d = 2.5$ ✗; $(1,1,4)$: $6 + d = 4d \Rightarrow d = 2 < c$ ✗; $(1,2,2)$: $5 + d = 4d$ ✗. Only $\{1,1,2,4\}$, with 12 arrangements.

**Answer: 12**
